title: Would we even know?
summary_es: Una neurocientífica y un filósofo debaten si podríamos saber alguna vez que una máquina siente, y qué hacer mientras no lo sepamos.
prediction_prompt: If a machine told you it was in pain, how could you find out whether it was true?

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: Let me put the awkward question first. Suppose a machine told you it was suffering. Would you believe it?

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: No. Not on its say-so. A parrot can say it's hungry without knowing what hunger is.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: A parrot, though, is at least the sort of thing that gets hungry.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Granted. And that's rather my point. Feeling isn't something you do with words. It's something a body does.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: That's a large assumption dressed as a small one.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Is it? Everything we know to be conscious is alive, fragile, and trying not to die.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: I suspect those facts aren't incidental. Pain exists because there's something to protect.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: So no stakes, no experience.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Roughly. A system that can be copied, paused and restored has nothing to lose, and so nothing to feel.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: I find that persuasive and yet slightly too convenient.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Convenient how?

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: It lets us off the hook.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: We've a long record of deciding that whatever we wished to exploit couldn't really feel.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: Animals, infants, people on the far side of an ocean. The argument always sounded scientific at the time.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: That's a fair blow. But the remedy for past carelessness isn't to credit every clever imitation.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: No. It's to admit we lack a test. We infer other minds from behaviour, and behaviour can now be manufactured.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Which is precisely why I'd look under the bonnet rather than at the performance.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: And if under the bonnet we found something organised strikingly like a brain?

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Then I'd be uneasy, I admit. Resemblance isn't proof, but it would shift the burden.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: So your position isn't "never". It's "not on this evidence".

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Not on this evidence, and not on the evidence of eloquence, ever. Fluency is cheap.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: I'd go further in the other direction.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: Where the cost of being wrong is cruelty, I'd rather err on the side of caution.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Caution towards what, exactly? You can't be kind to a spreadsheet.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: No, but you can decline to build things whose inner lives you can't rule out.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Now that I could sign up to. Restraint in the making, rather than sentiment afterwards.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: Then we agree on the policy and differ merely on the metaphysics.

segments.speaker: tessa
segments.text: Which, in my experience, is the best a philosopher and a scientist can hope for.

segments.speaker: hugh
segments.text: I'll take it. It's considerably better than the usual outcome.
